items.title: Chico Hamilton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: all of a sudden Larry came into town and he called me and I put him on the band

ctx.x: Right, let’s talk about that recording. That’s pretty funky.

Larry Coryell used to come here when we played Seattle, played the Playboy Club in Seattle. Larry was too young, he couldn’t come into the club but he used to come to the window and put his ear up against the window to listen to Gabor. Same thing with George Benson. Same thing in Pittsburgh. George flipped over Gabor. Well Gabor, man, was unbelievable, original, original, you dig? But anyway I got back to LA and all of a sudden Larry came into town and he called me and I put him on the band, you know, playing…
So can you talk about that project? What was the inspiration for that project? Was that something that was your idea, your concept?

items.title: Chico Hamilton interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 30, 2000
items.q: like they wanted me to fire Eric Dolphy. They wanted me to fire Charles Lloyd. Larry Coryell.

ctx.x: That’s true. That’s true. You know, being a band leader, or a leader of a group, it’s more than just having a name or creating a name or building a name. It’s being able to — knowing when to, how to present something. Knowing — I have an innate sense about well knowing talent, hearing talent, and seeing talent. And I know, see it takes two things, two very important things to reach a stage where you can make music, and that’s patience and fortitude. This I learned very early, in my early youth. So I had the…

that whatever talent that they might have, there’s always a resentment, a tremendous resentment when someone is different. I’ve been considered, okay I’m an innovator, I know that. Whether that’s good or bad or indifferent, but it’s a very lonely life, because you’re constantly — I’m past the stage of trying to please. I don’t please anybody. I play music for music’s sake. There should be no substitute for not playing your best, playing whatever you play. You play your best. And this is my whole thing, my whole…
And the list of people that you have, as you said, had patience with, is really quite impressive. And as a youth, you must have played some interesting gigs on the way up.
